blurb: A vase-shaped clump of thread-fine dissected leaves carrying golden daisies in profusion over a very long season. Known across the Southwest as Navajo tea or cota — the dried plant makes a smoky, faintly sweet beverage with centuries of use behind it.
water: Low; xeric — well-drained ground, little or no supplemental water once established
seasons: Profuse golden daisies from midsummer to frost over finely dissected foliage; dies back in winter
wildlife: Native bees and butterflies work the flowers

care.hardiness: CSU lists this as a Colorado native plantable to about 8,000 ft, so cold is not the constraint at Boulder's zone 5b–6a.[1]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, or in early fall, into ground prepared to suit it (see Soil). Set out young container plants — most of these natives resent having an established root system disturbed — and water them in well, then taper off.[1][2]
care.sun: Full sun, which is CSU's exposure rating for it.[1]
care.soil: Well-drained soil — dry, sandy, clay or rocky ground all suit it. This is a plains and Southwest plant that asks for drainage and heat, not fertility.[1][3]
care.water: Low. CSU rates its moisture requirement low, and on the semi-arid Front Range that is the number that matters most — the commonest way to kill a xeric native here is kindness with the hose.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space to suit its mature spread of 12–18 in wide. A vase-shaped clump with finely dissected leaves and profuse daisy-like flowers over a long period.[1]
care.propagation: By seed, which is how nearly all of these natives are raised and how they persist in a planting. Autumn sowing outdoors lets winter provide the chilling most of them want.[1]
care.bloom: Flowers from midsummer through to frost; CSU records the colour as yellow and the height as 16–24 in tall.[1][3]
care.maintenance: If you want it for tea, cut whole stems while it is in flower and dry them in bundles out of direct sun; the traditional preparation uses the dried leaves and stems rather than fresh material. Otherwise just let it bloom and reseed — it is one of the longest-flowering natives on CSU's list.[1][3]
care.troubles: Few pests or diseases when it is sited right. Crown and root rot in soil that stays wet is the usual cause of failure for a Colorado native in a Front Range garden, and it is a siting problem rather than bad luck.[1][2]

UTEP Herbal Safety — Cota (Thelesperma, greenthread/Navajo tea)

edible.card: Dried leaves & stems for tea (Navajo tea / cota)
edible.summary: A genuine, long-documented tea plant: the dried leaves and stems make the Southwestern beverage known as Navajo tea, Hopi tea or cota.[1][3]
edible.caution: This is a real and long-used beverage plant — Navajo, Hopi, Apache and Pueblo communities have made tea from greenthread for centuries, and several *Thelesperma* species are used interchangeably for it. Sensible limits. It is a tea herb, not a vegetable: use the dried leaves and stems as an infusion rather than eating the plant. The traditional record also describes it as a mild diuretic, so it is not a drink to take in unlimited quantity, and there is no established dose — if you are pregnant, nursing or on medication, treat it as you would any herbal infusion and check first. It is an Asteraceae, so daisy-family allergies apply. Harvest only from plants you have grown or can confirm are unsprayed, and identify carefully before drinking anything.[1][3]
